subtopic: Moving to a new city on limited money
subtype: Approach: build a local routine and support circle within a month [Action]
passage:
Day 3. Sharmila reached Pune with one suitcase and a tight monthly budget, and dinner was biscuits because the lane had no kitchen she trusted. A colleague, Tanuja, scribbled the name of a lady who packed home-style lunch boxes and dinners for a fixed monthly amount.

Day 11. The box now arrived every evening at seven. The lady's daughter mentioned a Saturday sketching circle in the park, and Sharmila went, holding her notebook like a shield. She came away with two phone numbers.

Day 27. She typed the landlord's number and a nearby doctor's number into her phone under names she could find quickly. That night the bathroom tap burst, and she reached the landlord within two minutes. The city felt smaller than it had a month earlier.

qa.q: Who gave Sharmila the name of the lady who packed lunch boxes?
qa.a: Tanuja, a colleague, scribbled the name for her.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she walked into the sketching circle holding her notebook like a shield?
qa.a: She was nervous and unsure among strangers, and the notebook held like a shield suggests she wanted some protection.

qa.q: If no colleague had offered a name, what other approach could have helped Sharmila settle in, and why?
qa.a: She could have asked the landlord or a nearby shopkeeper which meal service people in the lane trust, because neighbours know what is reliable and affordable. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tanuja have seen Sharmila's first weeks in the city?
qa.a: Tanuja likely saw a newcomer who only needed one small push, since passing on a single name cost little but opened the way to a routine.

grounding: Sharmila builds a meal routine, a weekend hobby circle and saved contacts for a landlord and a doctor over about a month.

subtopic: Moving to a new city on limited money
subtype: Approach: build a local routine and support circle within a month [Action]
passage:
Nitin, you've been eating biscuits for dinner since you came to Kolkata, haven't you? I can tell. Let old Raghav tell you what I did in my first month here, twenty years ago, when I didn't know a single soul.
First week: I found a tiffin aunty two lanes away. Rice, dal, one sabzi, every evening at eight. Not fancy. But I knew dinner would come.
Second week: I joined a Sunday morning chess group in the park near Deshapriya. Retired uncles and college students, arguing over every move. I went every Sunday, even when I lost.
Third week: I wrote three numbers on a card in my wallet. The doctor at the corner clinic, the landlord, and the tiffin aunty, because she knew everyone.
In the fourth week I got a fever. The tiffin aunty sent soup, and one of the chess uncles drove me to the doctor. By then the city wasn't strange any more. So, Nitin. Tiffin first. Go.

qa.q: Where did young Raghav's chess group meet?
How might young Raghav have felt when the fever came in the fourth week?
qa.a: Unwell and a little scared, but relieved and cared for when the tiffin aunty and a chess uncle stepped in.

qa.q: Which step in the story mattered most when the fever came, and why?
qa.a: Building the small network, the tiffin aunty and the chess group, since they sent soup and got Raghav to the doctor.

qa.q: How might the tiffin aunty have seen young Raghav?
qa.a: As a lonely regular she could look out for, which is why soup arrived when Raghav fell ill.

grounding: Shows a newcomer finding a tiffin service, joining a weekend group and saving a doctor's and landlord's numbers, so the city becomes manageable.

subtopic: Moving to a new city on limited money
subtype: Approach: build a local routine and support circle within a month [Action]
passage:
Kishore arrived in Guwahati in June with two bags, a job at a pharma warehouse and not a word of Assamese. The monsoon started the same week. For ten days he ate at a different stall each night, got lost twice, and felt like a visitor.
So he made a list and gave himself a month. Week one: a tiffin service. His colleague Jagdish pointed him to a woman near Zoo Road who sent rice, dal and fish curry for ₹2,800 a month. Week two: a hobby. He found a Saturday football group on a college ground, and played in ankle-deep mud with students who taught him three Assamese words a game. Week three: he saved numbers on his phone and on paper: a clinic doctor near his lane, the landlord, Jagdish.
In week four, when water entered the ground floor of his building, he knew exactly whom to call first. The landlord came with sandbags. The football group came with a spare mattress.

qa.q: How much did the tiffin service cost?
How did Kishore feel in his first ten days?
qa.a: Lost and lonely, like a visitor in a strange city, eating at a different stall every night.

qa.q: What else could Kishore add to his local circle?
qa.a: More of the language from the football group, and introductions to neighbours, so help is close by in the next flood too.

qa.q: What might the football group get from having Kishore join?
qa.a: A keen new player to teach words to, and the chance to help a newcomer, which they do with the spare mattress.

grounding: Shows a newcomer building a tiffin routine, a weekend hobby group and a list of emergency contacts within a month in a strange city.
